steps.observation: Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Key differences between DNA and RNA

1. Sugar
• DNA: Deoxyribose (lacks an ­OH on the 2′ carbon).  
• RNA: Ribose (has an ­OH on the 2′ carbon).  
   – Consequence: The extra 2′-OH makes RNA more chemically reactive and less stable than DNA.

2. Bases
• DNA: Adenine (A), Guanine (G), Cytosine (C), Thymine (T).  
• RNA: A, G, C, Uracil (U) in place of thymine.

3. Strandedness & structure
• DNA: Typically double-stranded, forming a long, antiparallel double helix (B-form in cells).  
• RNA: Usually single-stranded, but it folds back on itself to create complex secondary/tertiary structures (hairpins, loops, ribozymes). Double-stranded RNA can exist transiently (e.g., siRNA, viral genomes) and adopts an A-form helix.

4. Size & length
• DNA: Entire genome—millions to billions of base pairs per chromosome.  
• RNA: Usually much shorter—tens to thousands of nucleotides (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA, miRNA, etc.). Some viral RNAs are longer.

5. Function
DNA: Long-term storage of hereditary information; template for replication and transcription.  
RNA: Multiple functional roles:
   – mRNA: conveys genetic code to ribosomes
   – rRNA, tRNA: core components of translation machinery
   – Regulatory RNAs: miRNA, siRNA, lncRNA
   – Catalytic RNAs (ribozymes) and self-splicing introns
   – Some viruses use RNA as their genetic material.

6. Cellular location
• DNA: Mostly confined to nucleus (eukaryotes), mitochondria, chloroplasts.  
• RNA: Synthesized in nucleus (or nucleoid) but functions largely in cytoplasm; also found in nucleolus, mitochondria, chloroplasts.

7. Stability & repair
• DNA: Highly stable; protected by histones, chromosome packaging, and repair systems.  
• RNA: Short-lived; rapidly degraded by ribonucleases; no extensive repair pathways.

8. Replication vs. transcription
• DNA replication is semiconservative and requires DNA polymerases.  
• RNA is made from DNA by transcription using RNA polymerases; RNA itself is not generally copied into more RNA in cells (except in RNA viruses).

9. Chemical modification
• DNA: Mostly cytosine methylation (5-mC) for epigenetic control.  
• RNA: Extensive post-transcriptional modifications (methylations, pseudouridine, 2′-O-methyl, etc.) that affect stability and function.

10. Evolutionary perspective
RNA is thought to have preceded DNA (RNA world hypothesis) because it can both store information and catalyze reactions.

Summary
DNA is the cell’s durable, double-stranded genetic archive built on deoxyribose and thymine. RNA, containing ribose and uracil, is usually single-stranded, more reactive, short-lived, and versatile—acting as messenger, adaptor, catalyst, regulator, and, in some viruses, the genome itself.
